title: docs: add decimal footgun section to use-arc skill
body:
## Summary

Small, focused addition to the existing `use-arc` skill: a new **Common Pitfalls → The Decimal Footgun** section that reinforces the existing decimal guidance with a concrete, real-world example.

## Motivation

Arc uses USDC as its native gas token, which makes it easy to assume *every* amount uses 18 decimals like a typical EVM chain — when in fact ERC-20 USDC uses 6 decimals and only native gas (`msg.value`) uses 18. This is a real trap: we hit exactly this decimal mismatch in one of our own projects (a USDC payment flow), where `parseEther` was used instead of `parseUnits(amount, 6)`, producing an amount 10^12 times too large. We wrote it up in a Paragraph article (https://paragraph.com/@coliseum/the-18-vs-6-decimal-footgun-on-arc-what-nearly-killed-coliseum) as a lesson learned, and this PR distills that experience into the skill so other builders (and agents) avoid the same mistake.

## What's added

- A concrete failure scenario with real numbers (`parseEther('10')` → 10^18 vs `parseUnits('10', 6)` → 10^6, a 1,000,000,000,000x error)
- A ❌ WRONG / ✅ CORRECT TypeScript/viem code comparison
- A one-line rule to remember
- A note on why it's dangerous: can revert on insufficient balance, or worse, silently succeed with a wildly wrong amount

## Consistency

This complements — and does not duplicate — the existing **"Dual decimals"** Core Concept and the **Best Practices** decimal rule. It follows the same markdown style, code-block conventions, and tone as the rest of the file.

title: Add a `circle-bundle` meta-skill for single-install coverage on Claude Desktop and other open source AI agents
body:
**Summary**

Currently, using the full Circle skill surface on Claude Desktop requires installing each of the 17 skills individually. There is no single-install path for desktop users who want complete coverage out of the box.

This issue proposes adding a `circle-bundle` meta-skill — a lightweight router `SKILL.md` that groups all existing skills under one installable entry point, with each sub-skill loaded on demand from a `references/` directory.

**Problem**

The existing install methods (`npx skills add` and `/plugin install`) work well in Claude Code and Cursor. Claude Desktop users, however, install skills by dropping `.skill` files or folder structures into their local skills directory. With 17 separate skills, that's 17 manual steps with no guarantee of consistency.

There is also no discovery layer — a user new to Circle's tooling has no single place to start before knowing which specific skill they need.

**Proposed Solution**

Add a new skill at `plugins/circle/skills/circle-bundle/` with the following structure:

```
circle-bundle/
├── SKILL.md          # Router + quick decision guide (~60 lines)
└── references/
    ├── use-usdc.md
    ├── bridge-stablecoin.md
    ├── use-gateway.md
    └── ... (symlinks or copies of existing skill files)
```

The `SKILL.md` stays lean — a routing table and a short decision guide (which wallet type, which transfer method, which agent wallet flow). Claude reads it first and loads only the relevant reference file for the task at hand, keeping context usage minimal.

**Benefits**

- Single install for Claude Desktop users
- Works as a discovery layer for developers new to Circle's tooling
- No duplication — reference files point to the same content as existing skills
- Follows the progressive disclosure pattern already used in the skill-creator reference implementation

**Notes**

I have already built and validated a working version of this bundle locally. Happy to open a PR with the implementation if the maintainers are open to the approach. I wanted to raise it here first to check fit before submitting code.

Thanks for the great work on this repo.

title: Proposal: Document destination settlement verification for BridgeResult mint flows
body:
## Summary

I did not find a single documented example that connects BridgeResult mint
metadata to destination receipt-level economic settlement verification.

The existing bridge guidance documents the CCTP lifecycle:

approve -> burn -> attestation -> mint

The USDC guidance documents transaction and transfer verification. A useful
combined pattern may be:

BridgeResult
-> mint step transaction hash
-> destination receipt
-> successful receipt
-> expected chain-specific USDC contract
-> exact recipient
-> exact amount
-> deterministic Transfer-log policy
-> settlement verified

This is a proposal for a small guidance/example addition, not a request for a
new App Kit or Bridge Kit API.

## Reproducible Arc Testnet example

I tested the pattern against a real Base Sepolia -> Arc Testnet CCTP V2 transfer.

Source burn:

`0xc3c0368632821d4656c1cba2348f0a338911ef6b7cacc2cb1d9a6cfb6e37169c`

Arc destination receiveMessage:

`0x02cc00bd06e3e87b8bf9a042bdad7d7c6b566a84b7bd3f14a4afdff85c404741`

Amount:

`1 USDC` (`1000000` base units)

Expected recipient:

`0x94705A9d675daa924F9190Eca4c05ED6B12d5345`

Arc Testnet chain ID:

`5042002`

Arc Testnet USDC contract:

`0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000`

The destination receipt was successful and contained one matching ERC-20
Transfer event from the expected USDC contract to the expected recipient for
exactly `1000000` base units.

The reference verifier returned:

`VERIFIED`

ArcScan:

https://testnet.arcscan.app/tx/0x02cc00bd06e3e87b8bf9a042bdad7d7c6b566a84b7bd3f14a4afdff85c404741

## Reference implementation

A small external reference implementation is available in:

https://github.com/Mabolla/arc-paylink

It is shared as a reproducible example, not as a request to adopt the
implementation or its API.

The reference covers:

- destination receipt success validation
- destination chain validation
- chain-specific USDC contract validation
- mint transaction hash validation
- ERC-20 Transfer event decoding
- exact recipient matching
- exact base-unit amount matching
- ignoring unrelated logs
- rejecting multiple exact matching logs deterministically
- rejecting reverted or indeterminate receipts
- standard destination-adapter mint flows only

It does not attempt to define Forwarder/Orbit-specific settlement semantics.

## Why this may be useful

A successful mint transaction proves that the destination mint call succeeded.
An application may still need to establish that the expected economic settlement
occurred.

For example:

- Was the destination receipt successful?
- Did the expected chain-specific USDC contract emit the transfer?
- Was the recipient exact?
- Was the amount exact in base units?
- Were unrelated logs ignored?
- Were ambiguous matching logs rejected?
- Was a reverted destination transaction treated as failure?

These checks are individually straightforward, but a short documented pattern may
help developers avoid treating “mint transaction succeeded” as equivalent to
“expected funds settled”.

## Question

Would this be useful as a small documentation/example addition to
`bridge-stablecoin`, or is there an existing preferred location for this
pattern?

If useful, I would be happy to prepare a small reviewable contribution that
follows the repository's existing conventions.

title: accept-agent-payments skill has no idempotency/retry-safety guidance for the exact high-frequency pattern it targets
body:
Read `plugins/circle/skills/accept-agent-payments/SKILL.md`, `references/testing.md`, and `references/express-integration.md` in full, plus searched open/closed issues for idempot/retry/duplicate (0 hits) before filing.

This skill's whole pitch is Gateway Nanopayments for "sub-cent, cent-level, high-frequency, or agentic API calls" — i.e. it explicitly targets the calling pattern most exposed to caller-side retry loops (agent hits a timeout/5xx/network blip mid-settlement and retries the same logical call). The entire integration surface it teaches is:

```ts
const gateway = createGatewayMiddleware({ sellerAddress: process.env.SELLER_ADDRESS! });
app.post("/summarize", gateway.require("$0.01"), handler);
```

— and the skill explicitly tells implementers *not* to think about the mechanics: "Do not hand-roll EIP-3009, EIP-712, signature verification, or settlement unless current Circle docs explicitly require it." `testing.md`'s full proof sequence is one unpaid 402 check + one `--estimate` + one paid call — there's no step anywhere (SKILL.md, testing.md, express-integration.md, or the Common Mistakes / Red Flags tables) that mentions what happens if a buyer's client retries after an ambiguous response, or whether `gateway.require()` de-dupes a repeated `TransferWithAuthorization` for the same logical purchase. A developer following this skill exactly, end to end, would ship a paid endpoint with zero awareness that retry-driven double-charging is even a risk category to check for — worse than an undocumented code path, since the skill actively discourages looking under the hood.

Not claiming `@circle-fin/x402-batching` itself lacks dedup internally (that's closed-source from what this skill exposes) — the gap is specifically that the *guidance* never tells the implementer to verify it, ask about it, or add a fallback if it's absent, even though "high-frequency agentic calls" is the skill's stated target case where this bites hardest.

**Working reference for the mechanism this guidance is missing:** we hit and closed this exact failure mode ("the infinite-loop wallet drain" — a non-deterministic retry signs a fresh authorization each pass, so N retries is N honest on-chain charges) in our own x402 seller stack. `Idempotency-Key` header / `_meta['x402/idempotency-key']` for MCP callers: a repeat of the same key by the same payer for the same item inside 24h returns the cached original result with no new settlement, scoped by `(surface, payer, hash-of-key)`, with the key additionally bound to a canonical hash (RFC 8785 JCS + sha256) of the request body so it can't be replayed against a different amount. Durable atomic admission claims the purchase intent before settlement even attempts, so a crash/timeout mid-flight can't race two attempts into two charges. Live for testing the shape: `POST https://scvd.store/api/conformance/v1`. Source if useful as a documentation reference: `src/lib/idempotency.ts`.

Suggested fix shape: a short "Retry Safety" subsection in SKILL.md (or a line in the Common Mistakes table) telling implementers to confirm whether Gateway's settlement path de-dupes retried authorizations, and if not, to add an idempotency key at the application layer before `gateway.require()` — same shape as the header contract above.

Filed as a documentation/completeness note, not a pitch.

— cv-scvd

title: docs(use-arc): add Common Pitfalls section with empirical gotchas
body:
Adds a new "Common Pitfalls" section to the \`use-arc\` skill capturing four real gotchas hit while building production-grade contracts and clients against Arc Testnet:

1. **Native USDC vs ERC-20 USDC decimals** — the most common bug. Agents default to \`parseUnits(amount, 6)\` because USDC is 6 decimals on every other chain. For native gas on Arc it must be 18. Includes wrong/right code examples + symptom description.
2. **\`eth_getLogs\` is capped at 10,000 blocks per call** — RPC error \`-32614: eth_getLogs is limited to a 10,000 range\`. Includes a chunked-backward enumeration pattern.
3. **\`waitForTransactionReceipt\` frequently times out** — Arc Testnet's RPC drops receipt-query connections for 30-60s windows. Treating timeouts as failures causes false-negative reports. Includes a poll-with-tolerance pattern + the "pre-compute deterministic IDs" trick.
4. **Avoid \`--private-key\` for long-running scripts** — the keystore-via-\`cast wallet import\` pattern. The current skill mentions this rule in passing in the Foundry block; this version adds the concrete \`cast wallet import deployer --interactive\` + \`forge script --account\` flow.

### Why this matters

The \`use-arc\` skill is the single piece of documentation an AI agent reads when generating Arc code. Currently it correctly states the rule "use 18 decimals for native gas amounts and 6 decimals for ERC-20 USDC amounts" — but doesn't give code examples showing what the wrong pattern looks like, or what symptoms it produces. Agents that read the rule still consistently produce \`parseUnits(amount, 6)\` because the prior "USDC is 6 decimals everywhere" is reinforced by ~8 chains of correct-elsewhere training data. Showing the wrong code → right code transition makes the skill behaviorally effective, not just descriptively correct.

The other three pitfalls (\`eth_getLogs\` cap, receipt timeout pattern, keystore over CLI flag) are operational realities of Arc Testnet that aren't documented anywhere agent-readable but bite every team building real applications.

### Source of these pitfalls

Encountered while building [Plinth](https://github.com/Ccheh/plinth) — a capital layer for AI trading agents on Arc — over the Agora Agents Hackathon (May 2026). All four patterns were debugged against the live testnet RPC; the code examples come from the working production codebase.

### Diff size

title: Add `secure-agent-payments` skill
body:
This adds a `secure-agent-payments` skill for hardening agents that spend money over x402 or the Circle agent wallet.

The existing agent-payment skills cover setup (`use-agent-wallet`), the pay flow (`pay-via-agent-wallet`), funding (`fund-agent-wallet`), and wallet-side spending limits (`agent-wallet-policy`). Wallet-side limits cap what a compromised agent can lose, but nothing today covers securing the agent itself: keeping keys out of the model's context, deciding whether a payment parameter that arrived from a web page or tool output can be trusted, re-verifying an endpoint before paying it, and enforcing budgets in the agent's own code. That inner layer is what this skill adds. It's written to complement `agent-wallet-policy` rather than replace it; the point is to have both.

What's in it:

- sign through the Circle agent wallet CLI session, so raw keys never end up in agent context, prompts, logs, or generated code
- a provenance gate for payment parameters from untrusted content (web pages, social posts, tool outputs, x402 discovery listings): they have to clear an allowlist, a direct 402 re-fetch, or human confirmation before the agent acts on them
- endpoint verification: re-request the 402 challenge from the canonical URL and check price, asset, and chain within tolerance, rejecting seller-driven redirects and price spikes
- per-payment, per-session, and per-minute budget caps enforced in code, with a kill switch
- append-only audit logging that never records secrets
- halting the payment loop on anomalies instead of retrying

These map to real incidents: key exfiltration (Banana Gun, ~$3M; a Telegram bot key leak, ~$200K; malicious MCP routers stealing credentials, ~$500K), prompt-injection drains (the Grok/Bankr reply injection, ~$200K; AIXBT via malicious social replies, ~55 ETH), and semantic manipulation of payment logic (Freysa, ~$47K through `approveTransfer`).

The skill follows the existing format: frontmatter with triggers, overview, prerequisites, quick reference table, core concepts, numbered implementation patterns in framework-agnostic TypeScript, security rules, next-step cross-references, reference links, and the standard disclaimer. Code stays generic (plain fetch and viem-style types), and volatile SDK details defer to the Circle MCP server. A row for the README skills table is included.

title: Rename mcp.json to .mcp.json so Claude Code loads the MCP server
body:
The plugin's MCP server config is currently at `plugins/circle/mcp.json`, but Claude Code only auto-loads plugin MCP servers from `.mcp.json` (dotfile). As a result, when users install `circle-skills` from the marketplace, the Circle MCP connector at `https://api.circle.com/v1/codegen/mcp` is not registered and the related skills can't talk to it.

Renaming to `.mcp.json` is a no-content change — the file's JSON is already valid Claude Code plugin MCP config.

Verified locally:
- `claude plugin marketplace add circlefin/skills`
- `claude plugin install circle-skills`
- Without rename: `mcp.json` is treated as a regular file; no MCP server is registered for the plugin.
- With rename: Claude Code picks up `.mcp.json` on install and the `circle` MCP server appears alongside the skills.

Reference: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/plugins

title: New skill proposal: `use-agent-economy`
body:
# New skill proposal: `use-agent-economy`

## Summary

This proposal requests a new skill that covers the full lifecycle of an
**autonomous agent as an economic subject** on Arc — identity, job
marketplace participation, reputation accumulation, and self-managed
treasury. None of the existing skills covers this end-to-end pattern;
builders currently have to stitch together four separate primitives
(ERC-8004, ERC-8183, Gateway, Modular Wallets) without guidance on how
they compose.

---

## The gap

The current skill catalog covers each primitive in isolation:

| Existing skill                      | What it covers                          |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| `use-arc`                           | Chain config, deployment, CCTP basics   |
| `use-gateway`                       | Unified USDC balance                    |
| `use-modular-wallets`               | Passkey wallets, ERC-4337               |
| `use-developer-controlled-wallets`  | Custodial payouts                       |
| `bridge-stablecoin`                 | CCTP crosschain transfers               |

There is no skill that addresses the **composition** of these primitives
for the "agent economy" use case — an agent that:

1. Has a persistent onchain identity (ERC-8004)
2. Competes for jobs and receives USDC on completion (ERC-8183)
3. Accumulates a verifiable, third-party reputation score (ERC-8004 ReputationRegistry)
4. Manages its treasury across chains autonomously (Gateway + Modular Wallets)

Builders following the Arc docs can register an agent identity (ERC-8004
quickstart) and separately run the ERC-8183 job lifecycle, but no
existing material connects the two or explains how reputation feeds back
into bidding strategy and treasury management.

---

## Proposed skill: `use-agent-economy`

**Location**: `plugins/circle/skills/use-agent-economy/SKILL.md`

### Sections

1. **When to use** — decision criteria vs. simpler skill options
2. **Layer 1 — Identity** — ERC-8004 registration, metadata schema for
   agent capabilities, token ID retrieval
3. **Layer 2 — Commerce** — ERC-8183 bid-to-fund pattern, deliverable
   hash commitment, USDC decimal rule
4. **Layer 3 — Reputation** — dynamic score calculation (not hardcoded),
   third-party recording, weighted composite score from event log
5. **Layer 4 — Treasury** — Gateway rebalancing, Modular Wallet with
   guardian threshold for large spends
6. **Full lifecycle example** — bootstrap once, handle jobs in a loop,
   scheduled treasury management
7. **Common mistakes** — self-reputation, 18-decimal USDC, no expiry,
   treasury drain, on-chain output storage
8. **Decision guide** — which Circle primitive maps to which agent need
9. **Related skills** — cross-references to existing skills

### Key decisions not covered anywhere today

- **Dynamic reputation scoring**: the ERC-8004 quickstart hardcodes
  `score: 95`. The proposed skill shows how to derive scores from real
  outcomes (error rate, latency, revision rounds) with domain-specific
  examples.

- **Self-dealing prevention**: ERC-8004 forbids the agent's own wallet
  from recording its reputation. This is a subtle protocol rule that is
  easy to violate; the skill makes it a first-class antipattern.

- **Gas reserve management**: agents that drain their entire USDC balance
  cannot pay gas on the next job. The skill recommends a minimum reserve
  and shows how to enforce it in treasury logic.

- **Guardian threshold pattern**: Modular Wallets support guardians, but
  the existing skill does not explain how to combine autonomous operation
  (below threshold) with human oversight (above threshold) for the same
  wallet.

---

## Draft SKILL.md

A complete draft is attached below. It is ready to use as-is or as a
starting point for the Circle team to refine.

[**View draft SKILL.md →**](https://github.com/circlefin/skills/files/...)

> Note: the draft will be added as an attachment or a pull request once
> the team confirms interest via this issue.

---

## Why this matters for the Arc ecosystem

Arc is explicitly designed for **agentic commerce** — the documentation
lists "AI-mediated marketplaces where agents buy, sell, and execute
transactions" as a first-class use case. ERC-8004 and ERC-8183 are
Arc-native standards for exactly this. A skill that makes it easy to
combine them reduces the time from "I want to build an agent economy app"
to "my agent is earning USDC on testnet" from days to hours.

---

## Checklist for the Circle team

- [ ] Review proposed SKILL.md structure and content
- [ ] Confirm ABI signatures for ERC-8004 / ERC-8183 match current
      testnet deployment
- [ ] Confirm Gateway and Modular Wallets SDK import paths
- [ ] Add to the skill table in README.md
- [ ] Optionally: add a sample application to `arc/references/sample-applications`

---

## About this proposal

Submitted by an independent developer exploring Arc + Circle Skills +
Claude Code on WSL. The draft was written using the Circle MCP server and
the existing quickstart documentation as source of truth. Any errors in
ABI signatures or SDK method names should be corrected against the live
Circle developer docs.
